resolution_table.mechanism: Feed barley substitutes for maize in EU and Black Sea rations when price-competitive, easing maize demand.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybean oil competes with rapeseed oil for global biodiesel/HVO feedstock demand; a tight soyoil complex pulls rapeseed oil and seed higher.

resolution_table.mechanism: Wheat competes with corn for feed-ration demand; lower-protein/feed-grade HRS substitutes into feed, so higher corn prices firm the feed-wheat floor and acreage, supporting HRS.

resolution_table.mechanism: Wheat and corn compete for feed-ration demand; higher corn prices pull feed wheat demand and lift the wheat-corn spread floor, supporting HRW.

resolution_table.mechanism: HRS (Minneapolis) is the high-protein milling substitute; HRS shortages divert milling demand to HRW protein, supporting KC price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Grain sorghum competes with HRW for southern-Plains acreage and feed/export demand, with ambiguous flat-price effect via relative returns.

resolution_table.mechanism: Palm competes with soyoil for biodiesel feedstock share; tight soyoil/RBD economics pull discretionary biodiesel toward palm, supporting price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Palm olein competes with soyoil for biodiesel and food blending share; tight soyoil economics pull discretionary demand toward palm, supporting olein.
resolution_table.blurb: High soybean oil prices shift Chinese food demand toward palm olein, raising its prices.

resolution_table.blurb: Soybean crush from China and South America determines domestic soyoil supply, the primary olein substitute, driving olein prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Rapeseed/canola oil is a substitute in Chinese cooking-oil demand; rapeseed tightness raises the call on palm olein as a replacement, lifting DCE price.

resolution_table.blurb: Abundant soyoil from high crush and imports captures cooking-oil share, pressuring rapeseed oil.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: Soybeans are crushed into meal; a higher imported soybean cost directly raises the input cost of DCE meal and lifts its price.
inverted_pairs_all.blurb: Higher imported soybean cost raises domestic meal input costs and prices.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: Soybeans are the raw feedstock crushed into soyoil; higher bean prices raise soyoil input costs (bullish) but also reflect more crush throughput that lifts soyoil output (bearish), so the net pass-through depends on oil share.
inverted_pairs_all.blurb: Higher soybean prices increase soyoil input costs but also boost output; net effect depends on oil's margin share.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: Soyoil is jointly produced from crushing imported soybeans; higher bean cost raises crush feedstock value and the floor under DCE soyoil price.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: Imported GMO beans (No.2) crushed for oil/meal can substitute non-GMO beans at the margin in lower-value uses; cheap No.2 caps the No.1 food-grade premium and pressures No.1 price.
inverted_pairs_all.blurb: Cheap imported crushed beans cap food-grade premiums and pressure prices.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: Raw and white (refined) sugar are tightly linked via the white premium (refining margin); a strong white premium incentivizes refiners to buy raws, pulling raw price up, and the two move together as substitutes for end demand.
inverted_pairs_all.blurb: Strong refining margins incentivize refiners to buy raw sugar, pulling raw prices up alongside white sugar.

qualifying_pairs.mechanism: Robusta substitutes for arabica in roaster blends and instant coffee; when arabica is dear, demand and price support flow to robusta, while a robusta supply shock can also pull arabica higher as the two compete for blend share.
qualifying_pairs.blurb: Arabica and robusta compete in blends; high arabica prices boost robusta demand and prices.

qualifying_pairs.mechanism: Corn-oil and the broader biofuel feedstock complex compete for renewable-diesel demand; corn/ethanol economics indirectly influence vegetable-oil pull on canola.
qualifying_pairs.blurb: Corn oil and vegetable oils compete for renewable diesel demand, affecting canola prices.

qualifying_pairs.mechanism: Corn competes with cotton for US/Brazil/India planting area; a higher cotton-to-corn new-crop price ratio pulls acreage to cotton, raising future corn-relative cotton supply.
qualifying_pairs.blurb: Higher cotton prices shift plantings from corn to cotton, reducing future corn supply.

qualifying_pairs.mechanism: Feed wheat and corn compete in EU livestock rations; higher corn prices (incl. Ukrainian corn availability) pull feed-wheat demand and raise the wheat-corn spread floor, supporting MATIF.

qualifying_pairs.mechanism: Wheat and corn compete for feed-ration demand; higher corn prices pull feed wheat demand and lift the wheat-corn spread floor, supporting HRW.

deck_eligible_pairs.mechanism: Soybeans and corn compete for the same US spring acreage; a higher corn price pulls acres away from soybeans, tightening soy supply and raising soy price.
